items.title: A fine-tuned 2015-era CNN beats GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 at diagnosing skin lesions, 62% to 42%
items.summary: The test used 200 lesions from the public MILK10k set, each confirmed by biopsy. Inception v3, fine-tuned on 68,011 ISIC images, got 125 first-choice diagnoses right. GPT-6 Astra got 84 and Fable 5.1 got 85, and the CNN was also ahead when counting a correct first or second choice (173 vs. 134 and 138).
items.why: General frontier models still lose to small specialist models in narrow visual domains that have lots of labeled data, which is the argument for vertical AI companies that own their own data.

facts.claim: A fine-tuned Inception v3 (2015 CNN) achieved 62% first-choice accuracy on 200 biopsy-proven skin lesions, beating GPT-6 Astra (42%) and Claude Fable 5.1 (42%).
facts.evidence: The CNN named the right diagnosis (out of 6 possiblities) for 125 of them (62%). The two frontier LLMs named it for 84 and 85 (42%).

facts.claim: Inception v3 was fine-tuned on 68,011 ISIC Archive images on a single H100 GPU for about twenty minutes.
facts.evidence: I used Inception v3 pretrained on everyday photographs and then fine-tuned all layers on 68,011 dermoscopic and clinical images from the ISIC Archive on a single H100 GPU... fine-tuned for about twenty minutes.

facts.claim: With a second-choice allowance, the CNN reached 173/200 correct vs 134 for GPT-6 Astra and 138 for Claude Fable 5.1.
facts.evidence: Allowing a second choice, it reached 173 of 200 against 134 and 138.

facts.claim: The CNN correctly identified 13 of 30 melanomas vs 8 for GPT-6 Astra and 11 for Claude Fable 5.1.
facts.evidence: It named 13 of the 30 melanomas against 8 and 11.

facts.claim: GPT-6 Astra over-called basal cell carcinoma (75 predictions vs 25 actual), including 14 of 30 melanomas; Claude Fable 5.1 over-called actinic keratosis (53 predictions vs 20 actual).
facts.evidence: GPT-6 Astra called 75 lesions basal cell carcinoma when 25 were, including 14 of the 30 melanomas, and Claude Fable 5.1 called 53 lesions actinic keratosis when 20 were.

facts.claim: Test designed and conducted by Dr Magnus Lynch, Consultant Dermatologist and Mohs Surgeon at Guy's Hospital and Honorary Reader at King's College London.
facts.evidence: Dr Magnus Lynch is a Consultant Dermatologist and Mohs Surgeon at Guy's Hospital and Honorary Reader (equivalent of Associate Professor) at King's College London.

context: Small sample: only 200 lesions (30 melanomas) — wide uncertainty on melanoma detection rates; single-run LLM evaluations (answers vary between runs).
MILK10k has been public since 2025, so LLMs may have seen it in training (which would help them); CNN test set was decontaminated.

Inception v3 is a baseline — state-of-the-art dermatology AI uses transformer ensembles on more data and performs considerably better; this is not a claim that CNNs beat all specialist AI, only that they beat these two frontier LLMs on this narrow task.

items.title: Notion's sixth-gen agent harness runs single tasks for 24+ hours, and seats now come with AI credits
items.summary: Notion rebuilt its agents on a queue-backed worker service, so tasks survive restarts and can run for more than 24 hours, up from five minutes. Agents also write scripts for browser work, compact long context, and have a separate "Review for me" model check risky actions. Business and Enterprise seats now include 1,500 Standard and 500 Select credits a month, and existing customers move over on November 2. Notion says its "Auto" router matched Opus 5.5 and Astra across 20+ use cases at about 90% lower average cost.
items.why: This is the seat-to-usage shift in practice: a seat buys a credit allowance, and a model router is what protects Notion's margin.

items.title: Open-weight models now serve about 72% of OpenRouter's tokens, up from about 28% a year ago
items.summary: Per Latent Space, weekly OpenRouter traffic is up about 27× since last November, to roughly 165T tokens. Closed models grew too (13× by one analysis), but their share fell from 74% to 28%. These figures cover only OpenRouter traffic, not the whole market.
items.why: Tokens and dollars are diverging. On Vercel's gateway in August, open models handled 56% of tokens but only 14 cents of every dollar, so high-volume work goes to cheap open models while the profit stays with closed frontier models.

items.title: GPT-6.1 Terra: OpenAI's mid-tier model gains 6 points and costs less than a third as much per task
items.summary: Terra costs $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output, versus $2/$12 for GPT-5.6 Terra. It is aimed at visual reasoning, computer use and writing, and is available in ChatGPT, Codex and the API. Artificial Analysis scores it 4 points below GPT-6.1 Sol overall, and its "makes up an answer when unsure" rate fell from 88% to 38%. OpenAI also says Terra meets the "Critical" cybersecurity level in its Preparedness Framework, so it ships with the same safeguards as GPT-6 Astra.
items.why: Mid-tier models decide what agents cost to run, and Terra's price undercuts open-weight competitors on the work where they have been gaining share (see Inference).

items.title: Update: Anthropic's IPO is reportedly about two weeks out, and nearly half its revenue comes through cloud marketplaces
items.summary: Reports put the Nasdaq listing ("ANT") around November 9. The widely quoted "$2T" is Polymarket's expected closing value, which slipped from about $2.1T to $2.0T after the filing; it is not a company target. New details from the S-1: about 48% of H1 2026 revenue (roughly $7.8B) came through Bedrock, Vertex and Azure Marketplace, up from 11% in 2023. The lockup releases shares in stages over more than a year instead of all at once after 180 days, and 5% of shares go into a Public Benefit Fund. Analysts' cash estimates range from about $132B to $134B.
items.why: The hyperscalers are Anthropic's compute suppliers and also its biggest sales channel, so a frontier lab's distribution now depends on the same three companies as its infrastructure.

items.title: Neoclouds sell off: CoreWeave falls 10% to a 52-week low as Nebius takes a one-year, $3.5B loan from Citi
items.summary: Nebius's 364-day secured loan from Citi costs SOFR + 2.75% and will fund data centers and GPUs. Nebius says it still has over $40B of investment-grade contracts it can borrow against. CoreWeave closed at $55.60 after Bernstein cut its target to $51, estimating CoreWeave needs about $85B to fund its committed backlog, and some CoreWeave bonds now yield around 15%, up from 9.675% when they were issued (per Motley Fool and press reports).
items.why: The GPU build-out runs on borrowed money, so the cost of that debt is now a real limit on how fast neoclouds can add capacity, whatever Jensen Huang says about demand being "off the charts."

items.title: Meta spent $34.9B on capex last quarter, and its free cash flow went negative
items.summary: Revenue rose 26% to $64.6B, but free cash flow was −$2.1B, down from $10.6B a year ago. Meta narrowed its 2026 capex guidance to $135–145B. Zuckerberg said more than 10M people in the US and Canada have set up the Muse assistant, that it isn't global yet because it needs so much compute, and that "it's going to be very important to get the math on all of this to work out."
items.why: A hyperscaler whose capex now exceeds its operating cash flow is one more reason AI infrastructure is moving to debt financing, the same pressure showing up in neocloud credit.

items.title: Update: OpenAI reportedly won Replit's model spending with a 30%+ discount on a $100M+/year contract
items.summary: The Information, citing one person familiar with the deal, says Replit moved most of its AI spending from Anthropic to OpenAI after OpenAI offered more than 30% off list prices. cases.label: Shivam's edit of the Kimi K3 provider-gap post (did well); he kept two of the brief's lines
cases.post:
Vals AI ran its legal benchmark against the same open-weight model Kimi-K3 twice, once through Moonshot and once through Baseten.

75.8% through Moonshot. 60.6% through Baseten.

The weights were identical. The serving wasn't. Quantization, chat templates and tool-call parsing all sit between the checkpoint and your API call, and Vals puts the cost of those choices at 15 points.

That is a bigger swing than most people expect from anything outside the model itself. Two providers can hand you the same file and a different product, and the same model card across both won't tell you which one you got.

With open weights, it's tempting to pick whichever provider has the lowest token price. But this benchmark comparison shows that the cheaper serving can cost real accuracy, so evaluate the model on the provider you'll actually use.

#opensource #openweight

cases.label: Shivam's edit of the skin-lesion data-moat post, hashtags cut from 4 to his usual 2
cases.post:
Is "data" a moat?
I get asked this question a lot.

Dr Magnus Lynch, a consultant dermatologist at Guy's Hospital, ran 200 biopsy-proven skin lesions past three models.

A fine-tuned Inception v3, Google's 2015 CNN, got 125 of 200 right (62%).

OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra got 84. Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 got 85. Both 42%.

The CNN was fine-tuned on 68,011 ISIC images on a single H100 for about twenty minutes.
It caught 13 of 30 melanomas. The LLMs caught 8 and 11. GPT-6 Astra predicted basal cell carcinoma 75 times when the true count was 25.

Two hundred lesions is small, and each LLM ran once. Inception v3 is a baseline, and state-of-the-art dermatology AI does better.

But a ten-year-old architecture fine-tuned on public labeled data beat two frontier models on a narrow visual task.

Twenty points on 200 biopsies is what a data moat looks like when you actually measure it.

In a nutshell, general frontier models still lose to small specialist models in narrow visual domains that have lots of labeled data, which is the argument for vertical AI companies that own their own data.

#ai #healthcare

cases.label: Shivam's rewrite of the open-models token-share post (also the logic prompt's bar), hashtags cut to 2; his "$3 job now under $1" example is his own illustration
cases.post:
Open models now handle 72% of the tokens on OpenRouter, up from 28% a year ago.

Total traffic grew about 27x in that time, to around 165T tokens a week. Closed models grew too, but open models grew much faster, so the closed share fell to 28%.

But more work doesn't mean more money. Vercel's AI gateway shows both. In August, open models handled 56% of its tokens but earned only 14 cents of every dollar.

So most of the money still goes to closed models. The likely reason: open models win cheap, high-volume work, and closed models keep expensive, lower-volume work.

That split only lasts while the top closed models are worth the extra price. And the gap is shrinking from both sides. Top models are getting cheaper - OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra costs $1 per million input tokens, half the $2 of GPT-5.6 Terra, and a job that used to cost $3 now costs less than $1. Cheaper models are also getting better.

Watch the 14 cents. It shows who is winning the money.

#ai #opensource

The token count isn't the story. It's the 14 cents.

#ai #opensource

cases.label: Broken "so": a conclusion the evidence contradicts
cases.post:
Vals AI ran its legal benchmark against the same open-weight model Kimi-K3 twice, once through Moonshot and once through Baseten.

75.8% through Moonshot. 60.6% through Baseten.

The weights were identical. The serving wasn't. Quantization, chat templates and tool-call parsing all sit between the checkpoint and your API call, and Vals puts the cost of those choices at 15 points.

So Baseten is the better pick for legal work. That is a bigger swing than most people expect from anything outside the model itself. Two providers can hand you the same file and a different product, and the same model card across both won't tell you which one you got.

With open weights, it's tempting to pick whichever provider has the lowest token price. But this benchmark comparison shows that the cheaper serving can cost real accuracy, so evaluate the model on the provider you'll actually use.

#opensource #openweight
